original_title: Segal AmeriCorps Education Award Tax Relief Act of 2026
plain_title: No Taxes on AmeriCorps Education Awards
plain_summary: People who complete a term of service in AmeriCorps can earn an education award (often called the Segal AmeriCorps Education Award) to help pay for college or pay off student loans. This bill would make that award tax-free, so it would no longer count as income on a person's federal taxes. For example, if a former AmeriCorps member used their award to pay down student loans, they would not owe federal income tax on that money.
key_provisions: AmeriCorps education awards would not count as taxable income
Award money used to pay off student loans would also be tax-free
Change applies to tax years ending after the bill becomes law
who_it_affects: People who serve in AmeriCorps and receive education awards would keep more of their award because they would not pay federal income tax on it.
why_it_matters: If you ever join AmeriCorps after high school to earn money for college or student loans, this bill would let you keep the full value of that award instead of losing part of it to taxes.
status_plain_english: This bill was just introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, so it hasn't been voted on yet.
latest_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

original_title: A bill to permit visiting dignitaries and service members from Taiwan to display the flag of the Republic of China.
plain_title: Letting Taiwan's Visiting Officials and Troops Show Taiwan's Flag
plain_summary: This bill would require the U.S. State Department and Defense Department to allow Taiwan's military members and government representatives to display Taiwan's flag and their military unit emblems. For example, a visiting Taiwanese soldier could wear a uniform with Taiwan's flag on it, and the flag could be shown at ceremonies or in State and Defense Department social media posts about working with Taiwan. The bill also says it does not change the long-standing U.S. 'One China Policy' toward China and Taiwan.
key_provisions: Requires the State and Defense Departments to permit display of Taiwan's flag and military unit emblems
Covers official uniforms, ceremonies or functions, and State and Defense Department social media posts about Taiwan
Applies to Taiwan's military members and representatives, including Taiwan's representative office in the U.S. (TECRO)
States that the bill does not change the U.S. One China Policy
who_it_affects: It mainly affects Taiwanese military members and officials visiting or working with the U.S., along with the U.S. State and Defense Departments that host them.
why_it_matters: The link to a high schooler's daily life is indirect, but the bill touches on U.S. relations with Taiwan and China, which can affect world trade, the products you buy, and global safety.
status_plain_english: A Senate committee approved a revised version of this bill, and it is now on the Senate's list of bills that could be brought up for a full vote, though no vote has happened yet.
latest_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 499.

original_title: Targeting Online Sales of Fentanyl Act
plain_title: Studying How Fentanyl and Other Drugs Are Sold Online
plain_summary: This bill would require the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a government watchdog agency, to study how fentanyl, other synthetic opioids, and meth are sold online. The study would look at how online drug sellers find and keep customers, how online platforms and payment services are used in these sales, how this affects people 18 and younger, and how well the government and tech companies are working to stop it. The GAO would have to report its findings to Congress within one year after the bill becomes law.
key_provisions: Requires a GAO study on online sales of fentanyl, synthetic opioids, and methamphetamine, with a focus on effects on people 18 and younger
Examines how federal, state, Tribal, local, and foreign governments and private companies work together to fight online drug sales
Reviews how online platforms use technology like machine learning to detect drug sales and penalize users
Requires a report to Congress within 1 year, including data on platform tips to the government and resulting arrests or convictions
who_it_affects: It would mainly affect the GAO, which must do the study, and could later shape how law enforcement agencies, social media and online companies, and young people online deal with illegal drug sales.
why_it_matters: Fentanyl sold through social media and other online platforms has reached teenagers, and this study, which focuses partly on people 18 and younger, could help guide future rules for keeping young people safe online, though the bill itself only calls for research and does not create new rules.
status_plain_english: This bill was just introduced in the House and sent to two committees, Energy and Commerce and the Judiciary, so it hasn't been voted on yet.
latest_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

original_title: Expressing support for the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement.
plain_title: Congress Backing the President's Exit from the Paris Climate Agreement
plain_summary: This is a resolution, which is a formal statement of Congress's opinion rather than a new law. It says Congress supports the President's action to pull the United States out of the Paris Agreement, the international climate deal adopted by countries in Paris, France, in December 2015. It does not create new rules, programs, or spending.
key_provisions: States that Congress supports the President's action to withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement
Defines the Paris Agreement as the climate decision adopted in Paris on December 12, 2015, under a United Nations climate treaty

why_it_matters: The link to a high schooler's daily life is indirect, but how the U.S. handles international climate agreements can shape energy policy, jobs, and environmental conditions in the future young people will live in.

original_title: ACE Veterans Act
plain_title: Letting Veterans Get a Full Year of Birth Control at Once
plain_summary: This bill would let veterans who get health care through the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) pick up a full year's supply of birth control at one time, instead of refilling it more often. It covers birth control pills, patches, vaginal rings, and other FDA-approved products used to prevent pregnancy. VA doctors who prescribe birth control would also have to tell veterans about this full-year option.
key_provisions: Veterans enrolled in VA health care can choose to fill a birth control prescription as a full-year supply
Covers pills, skin patches, vaginal rings, and other approved birth control products
VA medical providers must tell veterans about the full-year option when prescribing birth control
who_it_affects: It would affect veterans enrolled in VA health care who use prescription birth control, as well as the VA doctors and pharmacies that serve them.
why_it_matters: For most high schoolers the link is indirect, but it could matter to anyone who joins the military in the future or has a family member who is a veteran, since it changes how easily veterans can get birth control.

original_title: A resolution commemorating the 50th anniversary of Southeast Asian refugee resettlement and the many contributions and sacrifices of Southeast Asian Americans to the United States.
plain_title: Honoring 50 Years of Southeast Asian Refugees Resettling in America
plain_summary: This is a Senate resolution, which is a formal statement of the Senate's views rather than a law, and it does not create programs or spend money. It marks 50 years since refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos began resettling in the United States after the Vietnam War and the Khmer Rouge genocide, and it honors the sacrifices and contributions of Southeast Asian Americans. For example, it notes that more than 1.2 million Southeast Asians came to the U.S. between 1975 and the mid-2000s, including Hmong and Lao people who helped U.S. forces during the 'Secret Wars' in Laos.
key_provisions: Commemorates 50 years since large-scale Southeast Asian refugee resettlement began in the U.S.
Honors Southeast Asian Americans who served and gave their lives on behalf of the United States

why_it_matters: The direct impact on a high schooler is small because it is symbolic, but it highlights a piece of U.S. history that shaped many classmates' families and communities, and it puts the Senate's views on refugees on the record.
status_plain_english: This resolution was just introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, so it hasn't been voted on yet.

original_title: Coast Guard Combat-Injured Tax Fairness Act
plain_title: Returning Wrongly Taken Taxes to Combat-Injured Coast Guard Veterans
plain_summary: A 2016 law fixed a problem where taxes were wrongly taken out of one-time payments (called severance pay) given to military members who left service because of combat injuries, but it was carried out through the Department of Defense. This bill extends that law to Coast Guard veterans, who usually serve under the Department of Homeland Security (and in the past served under the Department of Transportation). Those departments would have to find the money that was wrongly withheld, report on it, and make sure it doesn't happen again.
key_provisions: Extends the 2016 Combat-Injured Veterans Tax Fairness Act to Coast Guard members when the Coast Guard is not part of the Navy
Requires the Secretaries of Homeland Security and Transportation to identify taxes improperly withheld from Coast Guard veterans' severance pay within one year
Requires those departments to carry out the law's reporting duties within one year
Requires Homeland Security to stop improperly withholding these taxes starting when the bill becomes law
who_it_affects: Coast Guard veterans who received severance pay after being injured in combat could have wrongly withheld taxes identified so they can get that money back, and the Departments of Homeland Security and Transportation would have new duties.
why_it_matters: The direct link to most high schoolers is small, but it matters for families of Coast Guard veterans and for anyone thinking about joining the Coast Guard, since it deals with how injured service members are treated financially.
status_plain_english: This bill was introduced in the House and sent to a smaller committee group that handles Coast Guard issues, so it has not been voted on yet.

original_title: National Gun Violence Research Act of 2025
plain_title: Funding More Scientific Research on Gun Violence
plain_summary: This bill would create a national program to study gun violence, including shootings, suicides, and accidental injuries and deaths involving guns. It would give out grants to colleges and nonprofits for this research, let health agencies like the CDC and NIH use their money to study gun violence, and require the government to share gun tracing data (records that track where guns came from) with researchers. For example, university scientists could get funding to study whether certain gun policies change suicide or homicide rates, and also how those policies affect people's ability to use guns for self-defense, hunting, and recreation.
key_provisions: Removes past limits on how federal gun tracing data can be used and requires sharing it with researchers under ethical rules
Allows health agencies like the CDC and NIH to fund gun violence research
Creates a National Gun Violence Research Program with a planning group and an advisory committee
Authorizes yearly grants from 2026 through 2031, including $25 million for health research and $15 million for National Science Foundation research
who_it_affects: It would mainly affect researchers, colleges, nonprofits, and federal agencies that study or track guns, and it could shape future gun safety policies that affect gun owners and communities.
why_it_matters: Gun deaths affect many young people and communities, and this research could influence future safety policies, though the bill itself funds studies rather than changing gun laws directly; it also could create research and training opportunities for college students.
status_plain_english: This bill was just introduced in the House and sent to three committees to review, so it hasn't been voted on yet.

original_title: Recognizing the history of the drug diethylstilbestrol and the harm it has caused, and for other purposes.
plain_title: Recognizing Harm Caused by the Drug DES and Creating an Awareness Week
plain_summary: This resolution recognizes the history of diethylstilbestrol (DES), a drug the FDA approved in the early 1940s and doctors gave to 5 to 10 million pregnant women until 1971 to try to prevent miscarriages. The drug was later linked to rare cancers in the daughters of women who took it, along with fertility, pregnancy, and other health problems. The resolution supports a 'DES Awareness Week' (April 20-26, 2025), backs restoring funding for a study that follows people exposed to DES, and urges the FDA to formally apologize to affected families.
key_provisions: Supports designating April 20-26, 2025 as 'DES Awareness Week'
Recognizes the history of DES and the harm it caused
Supports restoring funding for the DES Follow-Up Study
Urges the FDA to formally apologize to families affected by DES
who_it_affects: It mainly concerns people whose mothers took DES while pregnant, their families, researchers studying DES effects, and the FDA, though as a resolution it expresses the House's views rather than creating new laws.
why_it_matters: The link to most high schoolers is indirect, but it raises questions about drug safety and how the government responds when an approved medicine turns out to cause harm, which can affect anyone's family health.
status_plain_english: This resolution was just introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, so it hasn't been voted on yet.

original_title: EXPERTS Act of 2025
plain_title: Changing How Federal Agencies Make Rules and Disclose Conflicts of Interest
plain_summary: Federal agencies, like those that oversee health, safety, and the environment, write detailed rules to carry out laws passed by Congress, and the public can comment on those rules. This bill would require anyone who submits a study to an agency during that process to reveal who paid for it, would fine public companies that knowingly submit false information, and would create a new government office to help ordinary people take part. It would also tell courts to generally go along with an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear law, set time limits on White House review of rules, and let agencies bring back rules that Congress previously canceled.
key_provisions: People submitting studies about a proposed rule must disclose who funded and reviewed them, and agencies must flag studies largely funded by the companies they regulate
Public companies that knowingly submit false information face fines of at least $250,000, and at least $1 million for repeat violations
Creates an Office of the Public Advocate to help the public participate in rulemaking, and requires agencies to respond in writing to petitions with over 100,000 signatures

Tells courts to defer to agencies' reasonable interpretations of unclear laws, limits White House review of major rules to 60 days (with one possible 30-day extension), and lets agencies reinstate rules Congress previously struck down
who_it_affects: It would affect federal agencies, companies and groups that try to influence government rules, courts that review those rules, and members of the public who want a say in how rules are made.
why_it_matters: The link is mostly indirect, but federal rules shape things like the safety of food, air, products, and workplaces, so this bill could change who influences those rules and how easily young people and their families can weigh in.
status_plain_english: This bill was just introduced in the Senate and sent to a committee, so it hasn't been voted on yet.

original_title: CLEAR Act
plain_title: Tougher Penalties for Using or Blocking Vehicles Against Federal Officers
plain_summary: This bill would add new federal crimes with penalties of up to 20 years in prison, a fine, or both. One covers using a vehicle to forcibly attack, resist, intimidate, or interfere with certain federal law enforcement officers doing their jobs. The other covers forcibly attacking, resisting, blocking, or interfering with those officers while they are doing their jobs in a federal law enforcement vehicle, such as using force to stop an officer's car from moving.
key_provisions: Up to 20 years in prison and/or a fine for using a vehicle to forcibly assault, resist, intimidate, or interfere with a federal officer
Up to 20 years in prison and/or a fine for forcibly assaulting, resisting, impeding, or interfering with a federal officer who is on duty in a federal law enforcement vehicle
Applies to officers of the Department of Homeland Security (which includes immigration agents) and the Department of Justice (which includes the FBI)
who_it_affects: It would affect people charged with forcibly interfering with Department of Homeland Security or Department of Justice officers involving vehicles, by raising the possible punishment, and it would add protection for those officers.
why_it_matters: For most high schoolers the link is indirect, but it could matter for anyone who drives or attends events where federal officers are working, because forcibly blocking or interfering with their vehicles could lead to a long prison sentence.
status_plain_english: This bill was just introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, so it hasn't been voted on yet.

original_title: Federal Food Administration Act of 2025
plain_title: Creating a New Federal Agency Focused Only on Food Safety
plain_summary: Right now, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) oversees both food and medicine. This bill would move the FDA's food responsibilities, staff, and funding into a new agency called the Federal Food Administration, inside the Department of Health and Human Services, led by a Commissioner of Foods picked by the President and approved by the Senate. The new agency would have to inspect food facilities on a set schedule. For example, factories that make baby formula would have to be inspected at least every 6 months.
key_provisions: Creates the Federal Food Administration within one year, headed by a Senate-confirmed Commissioner of Foods
Requires inspections based on risk: high-risk food facilities every year, intermediate-risk every 2 years, low-risk every 3 years, and infant formula factories every 6 months
Requires state officials to carry out at least half of inspections and a follow-up check within 30 days after problems are found
Transfers the FDA's food-related powers, offices, and funding to the new agency
who_it_affects: It would affect food companies, factories, and warehouses that would face scheduled inspections, FDA workers whose food-related jobs would move to the new agency, state inspectors, and anyone who eats food sold in the U.S.
why_it_matters: The food you eat at home, in the school cafeteria, or from stores is covered by federal safety rules, so this bill would change which agency is in charge of checking that food is safe and properly labeled.

original_title: Fostering the Future for American Children and Families Act
plain_title: Helping Foster Youth Get Job Training and Apprenticeships
plain_summary: This bill would turn parts of a presidential executive order into law to help young people who are in or have left foster care get job training. key_provisions: Federal study of job training and apprenticeship programs for current and former foster youth, with a report to Congress within 1 year
Creates the Fostering the Future Pipeline Program, offering competitive grants of up to $50 million per year
Allows Chafee education and training vouchers to pay for short-term career programs, certificates, and apprenticeships
Takes effect 6 months after becoming law

why_it_matters: For teens in or leaving foster care, this could make it easier to get paid job training or a career certificate without going to a four-year college; for other students the effect is indirect.
